title: The Innocence of Father Brown
author: G. K. Chesterton
summary: Um padre católico baixinho, desajeitado e de guarda-chuva velho parece a pessoa menos perigosa da Inglaterra. Mas por trás do rosto simples do Padre Brown existe uma mente afiada que entende os criminosos melhor do que a polícia. Nestas quatro histórias, ele enfrenta um ladrão genial, um jardim fechado com um corpo sem cabeça, um assassino que ninguém consegue ver e um crime misterioso numa pequena aldeia.

chapters.title: The Blue Cross: A Strange Trail
paragraphs: On a silver morning, a boat arrived at the little English port of Harwich. Among the passengers was a man in a grey suit who looked like any other tourist. Nobody guessed that he was Aristide Valentin, the head of the Paris police and the most famous detective in Europe. He had come to England to catch the greatest criminal of the age: Flambeau.

Flambeau was a giant of a man, very tall and very strong, and he was clever as well. He had stolen jewels, cheated banks and once painted all the numbers on a street so that a family walked into a trap. Valentin knew that Flambeau was in England, and he knew one more thing. A precious silver cross with blue stones was travelling to London for a great meeting of priests. Flambeau would surely try to steal it.

On the train, Valentin looked carefully at every passenger. A tall man could hide in many ways, but he could not hide his height. There was nobody tall enough. There was, however, a very short Catholic priest from a small village in Essex. He had a round, simple face, a large shabby umbrella, and several brown paper parcels which he kept dropping on the floor. He told everyone in the carriage, “I must be careful. I’m carrying something made of real silver, with blue stones in it.” Valentin felt sorry for him. “What a fool,” he thought. “Anyone could rob a man like that.”

In London, Valentin had no idea where to look. So he followed his own strange method. When a detective has no clue at all, he said, he should go to the places that look wrong. He walked through the streets until he came to a small restaurant. Something about it seemed odd, so he went in and ordered coffee.

When he put sugar in his coffee, he made a face. It was salt. He looked at the salt cellar and tasted it. It was full of sugar. Then he noticed a dark stain on the wallpaper. “Waiter,” he said, “is this a joke?”

The waiter was nervous. “It’s very strange, sir. Two priests came in this morning. They had soup, and then the short one paid and walked out. But before he left, he picked up his cup and threw the soup at the wall! The other priest went with him. They turned into Carstairs Street.”

Valentin paid and ran out. At the end of the street he found a fruit shop. The label on the nuts said “Best oranges, two a penny”, and the label on the oranges said “Finest nuts”. The angry shopkeeper said that a little priest had knocked over his apples and gone on towards Hampstead with a very tall priest. Valentin called two policemen and took a taxi.

Further on, they saw a restaurant with a broken window. The manager explained, “Two priests had lunch here. The small one paid too much. I told him so, and he said it was for the window. Then he broke it with his umbrella!” At a sweet shop, the girl said the little priest had left a parcel by mistake and later sent a message asking her to post it to an address in Westminster. Valentin’s face became serious. He did not understand the game, but he knew he was close.

chapters.title: The Blue Cross: Reason and the Two Priests
paragraphs: It was evening when Valentin and the two policemen reached Hampstead Heath. The sky was a beautiful green and gold, and the grass was quiet. Far away, on a bench under a tree, they saw two black figures. One was very tall. The other was very short. Valentin and his men moved closer, hiding behind the trees, until they could hear every word.

To his surprise, the two priests were talking about the stars and about reason. “The stars are so far away,” said the tall one. “Perhaps in other worlds reason is different. Perhaps there two and two make five.”

“No,” said the little priest calmly. “Reason is the same everywhere. Even in the most distant star, God is reasonable. On those other worlds there may be trees with leaves of diamonds, but you will still find a law that says, ‘Thou shalt not steal.’”
Valentin was disappointed. “I have followed two silly priests across London,” he thought. “They are only talking theology.” He was ready to leave. But suddenly the tall priest’s voice changed.
“All right,” said the tall man roughly. “Give me that blue cross. We’re alone here, and I could pull you to pieces like a doll.”

“No,” said the little priest, in the same calm voice. “You can’t have it, Flambeau. I know who you are. And the parcel you took from me on the train is not the cross. It’s just a packet of paper. I changed the parcels.”
Flambeau laughed. “I knew you would try that. So I changed them again! I’ve got the real one in my pocket.”

“Have you?” asked Father Brown, for that was the little priest’s name. “Look in it.” Flambeau opened his parcel. Inside there was only paper and lead. “I changed them back,” said Father Brown gently. “The real cross is safe. I left it at the sweet shop, and they have posted it to a friend of mine in Westminster.”
Flambeau stared at him. “But how? How did you guess I wasn’t a priest?”

“I have heard a lot of confessions,” said Father Brown. “When you hear the secrets of murderers and thieves, you learn about evil. I suspected you as soon as we met, because you had a bracelet with a spike on your arm. Then you attacked reason. That is bad theology. A real priest never attacks reason.”
“And the salt, the soup, the window?” asked Flambeau. He could not stop himself.

“I wanted somebody to follow us,” said Father Brown. “I couldn’t call the police, because you would hurt me. So I left a trail. I changed the salt and sugar. I threw the soup at the wall. I paid for the window before I broke it, so nobody lost any money. Every time, people remembered two priests. And now, I think, the police are behind those trees.”

Flambeau jumped up like a wild animal. But three men stepped out of the shadows. Valentin was smiling. He did not look at the criminal. He took off his hat and bowed low to the little priest from Essex.
“Let us bow to our master,” said the great detective. Behind them, Flambeau, the king of thieves, stood still in the green evening light, and for once he had nothing to say.

chapters.title: The Secret Garden: A Body in the Garden
paragraphs: Some years later, Aristide Valentin, the chief of the Paris police, gave a dinner party at his house. It was an old house with a large garden, and the garden was very private. High walls with sharp spikes on top surrounded it, and the only way into it was through the house itself. Valentin was proud of this. “Nobody can enter my garden without passing my front door,” he often said.

His guests that evening were an interesting group. There was Lord Galloway, an old English ambassador, with his wife and his beautiful daughter, Lady Margaret. There was Commandant O’Brien, a handsome Irish soldier from the French Foreign Legion, who was in love with Lady Margaret. Her father did not like him at all. There was Dr Simon, a famous French scientist. And there was a little Catholic priest from Essex, Father Brown, whom Valentin had met in England.

The most important guest was Julius K. Brayne, an American millionaire. Brayne was famous because he gave enormous amounts of money to new religions and small churches. People said that he was thinking of becoming a Catholic, and that he might give millions to the Church in France. Valentin did not believe in God, and he did not like this news at all.

Valentin arrived late to his own dinner. He apologised and said he had been busy with work. After dinner, the guests moved around the house. Lord Galloway was in a bad mood, because his daughter and O’Brien had both disappeared. He went out into the garden in the moonlight to look for them.

Suddenly he stopped. Something was lying on the grass. It was the body of a tall man in evening dress. Galloway bent down and turned it over. Then he cried out in horror. The head was completely cut off. It lay a little way from the body, with grey hair and a strange, ugly face.

Galloway ran into the house shouting for help. Valentin came at once with Dr Simon and Father Brown. The doctor looked at the body. “The head was cut with one great blow,” he said. “Only a very strong man could do this, with a very heavy sword.”

“But who is he?” asked Valentin. Nobody knew the dead man. He was not one of the guests, and none of the servants had ever seen him. Valentin was very serious now. “How did he get into the garden? No one can come in except through the house, and my servant at the door says no stranger arrived tonight.”
Father Brown was looking at the head with sad, thoughtful eyes. “It is very strange,” he said quietly. “A man has been killed in a garden where nobody can come in. And he is a man that nobody knows.”

Then Lord Galloway spoke angrily. “I saw someone in the garden earlier. It was O’Brien! He was walking near the wall, and he looked very upset.” At that moment, O’Brien and Lady Margaret came in from the garden. The Irishman’s face was pale. Valentin looked at the commandant’s belt. His long cavalry sword was missing.
“Where is your sword, Commandant?” asked Valentin.
O’Brien stared at him. “I left it in the hall,” he said. But when they looked, it was not there.

Then a servant came with more news. Mr Brayne had gone. His hat and coat were not in the hall, and nobody had seen him leave. Valentin sent policemen to search the whole city. Everybody waited in the house, afraid and silent. Only Father Brown seemed to be thinking about something else. He kept looking at the dead man’s head, as if it were trying to tell him a secret.

chapters.title: The Secret Garden: Two Heads and One Body
paragraphs: Early the next morning, the police came back with terrible news. They had found a second head in the river, near Valentin’s house. It was the head of Julius K. Brayne, the American millionaire. And in the garden, under some bushes, they found O’Brien’s sword, covered in blood.
Lord Galloway was almost happy. “There you are!” he said. “It was the Irishman. He killed both men with his sword.”

But Lady Margaret stood up. Her face was white, but her voice was strong. “No,” she said. “Commandant O’Brien was with me in the garden all the time. He asked me to marry him, and I said no, because of my father. He was very unhappy, but he never left my side.” Her father was shocked, but nobody could doubt her.

Dr Simon shook his head. “Then we have a strange puzzle. Two heads and only one body. Did the killer cut off Brayne’s head and throw it into the river? Then where is Brayne’s body? And who is the stranger in the garden?”
Father Brown had been very quiet. Now he went pale and put his hand on his face. “Oh, God help us,” he said. “I have been so stupid. Let me see the body again.”

They went to the room where the body lay. Father Brown looked at the neck, then at the shoulders and the clothes. “Doctor,” he said, “is this body really the body of a man with grey hair and that ugly face? Look at it. Look at the shoulders. This head does not belong to this body.”
Dr Simon looked again, and his eyes opened wide. “You are right! This head was cut off a long time before the body was killed. Hours before.”

“There is only one body,” said Father Brown slowly. “It is the body of Julius K. Brayne. The killer cut off Brayne’s head and threw it into the river. Then he put another head next to the body. A head that he brought into the garden himself. That way, nobody would know that the dead man was Brayne. Everybody would think a stranger had died.”
“But where can anyone get a head?” cried Galloway.

“In Paris, it is easy,” said Father Brown sadly. “Yesterday a criminal called Becker was executed. The guillotine cut off his head. A man who works with the police could take that head and carry it in a bag. A man who arrived late to his own dinner. A man who owns the house and the garden, and who could walk out into it whenever he wanted.”

Everybody turned. Valentin was not in the room. “He hated religion,” Father Brown continued. “He could not bear the idea that Brayne would give millions to the Church. So he killed him with O’Brien’s sword, and he tried to make us think the killer was the Irishman.”

They ran to Valentin’s study. The great detective was sitting at his desk. He was dead. On the desk was a small empty bottle of poison. The most famous policeman in Europe had judged himself, and he had found himself guilty.
Father Brown stood at the door for a long moment. Then he bent his head and quietly said a prayer for his old friend.

chapters.title: The Invisible Man: The Letters on the Window
paragraphs: In Camden Town, in north London, there was a small cake shop on a corner. On a cold winter afternoon, a young man with red hair walked in and sat down. His name was John Turnbull Angus. He ordered a coffee and a cake, and then he looked at the pretty young woman behind the counter.
“And I’d also like you to marry me,” he said.
Laura Hope laughed, but then she looked serious. “I can’t answer that yet,” she said. “First I must tell you a strange story. Sit down and listen.”

She explained that a few years before, she had worked in her father’s inn in the country. Two men had both wanted to marry her. One was Isidore Smythe, a very small man who was always making jokes. The other was James Welkin, a tall, silent man with a terrible squint in one eye. Laura did not love either of them. So she told them a little lie. “I can only marry a man who has made his own fortune,” she said. Both men left to find their fortunes.

“And now,” Laura said, “Isidore Smythe is rich. You have probably heard of Smythe’s Silent Service. He makes machines that work like servants. They carry food, open doors, and clean the house. They are in all the newspapers. He writes to me often. But Welkin I have never seen again. And yet...” She looked frightened. “Sometimes, when I’m alone, I hear his laugh. It’s very close, but there is nobody there. And once, when Smythe’s letter arrived, I heard Welkin’s laugh again. Do you think I’m going mad?”

Before Angus could answer, the door opened. A tiny man in an expensive coat came in. It was Isidore Smythe himself. He seemed angry and afraid. He pointed at the shop window. On the outside of the glass, somebody had stuck a strip of paper. It said: “If you marry Smythe, he will die.”

“That wasn’t there five minutes ago,” said Angus. “I was sitting here. Nobody came near the window.” He ran out into the street, but there was nobody suspicious, only the usual people walking past in the snow.
Smythe was pale. “I’ve been getting letters like this for weeks,” he said. “They are in Welkin’s writing. They appear in my flat, and nobody sees who brings them. I think he wants to kill me.”

Angus was a practical young man. “I have a friend who can help,” he said. “His name is Flambeau. He was once a famous thief, but now he works as a private detective. He lives near here. Let’s take you home first, and then I’ll fetch him.”

Smythe lived in a very modern block of flats called Himalaya Mansions, at the top of a hill. When they arrived, Smythe’s little mechanical servants stood in the hall like strange, headless dolls. On the floor of the flat lay another letter in red ink: “If you have seen her today, I will kill you.”

Angus thought quickly. “Lock your door and stay here,” he told Smythe. “I’ll make sure nobody can get in.” Outside, he spoke to four people. The porter promised to watch the main door. A policeman agreed to watch the street. A man selling hot chestnuts promised to look at everybody who passed. And a commissionaire stood at the gate of the building. “Watch everybody,” Angus said. “Nobody must go in.” Then he hurried off through the snow to find Flambeau.

chapters.title: The Invisible Man: Footprints in the Snow
paragraphs: Flambeau lived in a flat near the canal. When Angus arrived, the big Frenchman was sitting by the fire with his friend, Father Brown, the little priest with the round face. Angus told them the whole story. Flambeau listened carefully, but Father Brown seemed more interested in the snow outside the window.
“We must go at once,” said Flambeau, and the three men walked quickly up the hill to Himalaya Mansions. It had stopped snowing, and the street was white and clean.
The commissionaire was still at the gate. “Has anybody gone in?” asked Angus.
“Nobody, sir,” the man said. “I’ve been here all the time.”
The policeman said the same, and so did the chestnut seller. “Not a single person has passed,” he said. “I’m sure of it.” The porter at the door shook his head too. “Nobody has come in or gone out.”
But Father Brown was looking down at the steps. “Then who made those?” he asked. In the snow there was a line of grey footprints, going up the steps and into the building, and then coming out again.

They ran upstairs. Smythe’s door was open. The little mechanical servants stood in the hall, but their master was not there. On the floor there was a red stain that looked like blood. Angus felt sick. “He’s been murdered,” he said. “But where is he? And how did the killer get in and out?”
“He was invisible,” said Angus in a low voice. “Laura heard his laugh when nobody was there. Perhaps Welkin really is a ghost.”
A few minutes later, the policeman came running up the stairs. “They’ve found a body in the canal,” he said. “A very small man, with a knife wound in his chest. It’s Mr Smythe.”

Angus sat down, shaking. Flambeau was silent. Father Brown was still looking at the stain on the floor, and suddenly he turned round. “Those four men outside,” he said. “Let me ask them one more question.”
He walked down the stairs and spoke to the commissionaire, the policeman and the chestnut seller. Then he came back with a strange, quiet smile.

“They all told the truth,” he said. “Nobody went in. But when people say ‘nobody’, they don’t really mean nobody. If a lady asks, ‘Is anybody staying in this house?’ the servant says ‘No,’ even if the cook and the gardener are there. The servant means nobody important. Nobody that the lady would want to know about. Some people are so ordinary that we do not see them at all. They are mentally invisible.”
“But who?” cried Angus.

“A man who goes into every building every day,” said Father Brown. “A man who carries letters. A man in a uniform, with a big bag on his back. Nobody notices him, but he can go anywhere.” He pointed through the window. Far down the street, a tall man in a postman’s uniform was walking away quickly with a heavy bag.
“The postman!” said Flambeau.

“Yes,” said Father Brown. “Welkin became a postman. That is how he put the letters in Smythe’s flat, and that is how he stuck the paper on Laura’s window. He killed Smythe and carried the small body out in his postbag. Smythe was so small that it was easy. Nobody looked at him, because nobody ever looks at the postman.”

Flambeau ran down the hill and caught the man. Father Brown walked beside the murderer for a long time that night, under the stars. Nobody knows what they said to each other. And a few months later, Angus came back to the cake shop on the corner, and this time Laura said yes.

chapters.title: The Hammer of God: Two Brothers
paragraphs: The little village of Bohun Beacon stood on top of a high hill. Its church had a very tall tower, so tall that people said you could see half of England from the top. Two brothers from the old Bohun family lived in the village, and they were as different as day and night.

The younger brother, the Reverend Wilfred Bohun, was the priest of the church. He was thin, pale and very religious. He spent hours every day praying, and he loved the old church more than anything. He often climbed the tower and prayed up there, high above the houses.

The older brother, Colonel Norman Bohun, was not religious at all. He was a big, strong man who drank too much and laughed at everything. He wore a strange green hat, and he was always looking for trouble. Everybody in the village knew that he was spending too much time with the wife of the blacksmith, Simeon Barnes.

Early one morning, Wilfred was walking to the church when he saw his brother. The colonel had been drinking all night. “Good morning, Wilfred,” he said with a laugh. “I’m going to visit the blacksmith’s wife. Her husband is away in the next town.”
“Norman, be careful,” said the priest. “Barnes is the strongest man in the district. If he finds out, he could kill you with one blow.”

“Barnes is a Calvinist,” said the colonel. “He’s too busy thinking about God.” He laughed again and walked away. Wilfred went into the church to pray. He was very angry, and very ashamed of his brother.
An hour later, a man ran into the church. It was the shoemaker. “Reverend, come quickly!” he said. “Your brother... Something terrible has happened.”

In the yard of the blacksmith’s house, Colonel Bohun was lying on his face. His strange green hat was crushed, and his head was smashed like an egg. Next to him lay a hammer, a very small, light hammer. A few people from the village stood around, silent and afraid. Among them was the local doctor, and a visitor who had come from a nearby town: a little Catholic priest called Father Brown.
The inspector arrived and looked around. “This was done with great force,” he said. “Only the blacksmith could hit a man like that. He is the strongest man for miles.”

But at that moment, Simeon Barnes himself walked into the yard. He was a tall, serious man with a red beard. He looked down at the body without fear. “I did not kill him,” he said calmly. “I have been in the next town since last night, with four good men who will say so. I left my house at dawn and came back just now. God sees everything. He will find the murderer.”
His four friends quickly agreed. It was true. The blacksmith could not have done it.

Then somebody pointed at a young man who was sitting by the wall, smiling foolishly. It was Mad Joe, a poor simple boy from the village. “He was here this morning,” somebody said. “He could have done it.”
The doctor shook his head. “That boy is not strong enough to break a man’s head like this.”

Father Brown had been quiet all this time. He picked up the little hammer and looked at it carefully. “This is a very small hammer,” he said. “A woman could use it. A child could use it. There are much bigger hammers here. Why didn’t the killer take one of those?”
Nobody answered. Father Brown looked up, past the roof of the blacksmith’s house, at the tall grey tower of the church.

chapters.title: The Hammer of God: At the Top of the Tower
paragraphs: Later that afternoon, Wilfred Bohun went back to the church. He felt sick and confused, and he wanted to pray. Father Brown followed him inside. “Mr Bohun,” he said gently, “would you climb the tower with me? I would like to see the view.”

The priest looked surprised, but he agreed. They climbed the narrow stone stairs for a long time, round and round, until they came out onto a gallery at the very top. The wind was cold. Far below, the village looked like a toy. The people in the streets were as small as insects, and the blacksmith’s yard was directly under them.
Father Brown looked down for a long time. “It is dangerous to be up here,” he said at last. “Even for a good man. Especially for a good man.”
“What do you mean?” asked Wilfred.

“When you stand so high,” said Father Brown, “you begin to see other people as insects. You begin to feel that you are not a man any more, but something greater. You look down on the world as if you were God. I think a man should pray on the ground, among other people. Humility is the mother of giants. From the valley, you can see great things. From the top of a tower, you see only small ones.”
Wilfred said nothing. His hands were holding the stone wall very tightly.

“The doctor said the blow was enormous,” Father Brown continued. “But the hammer was tiny. How can a small hammer break a man’s head like that? There is only one way. If it falls from a great height, a very small thing hits with terrible force. Like a stone from the sky. Like the hammer of God.”
Now Wilfred’s face was as white as paper. “I...” he began.

“I think a man came up here to pray,” said Father Brown softly. “He was a good man, but he was full of anger. He saw his brother below, going into the yard of the blacksmith’s wife, wearing that green hat. The brother looked like a small green insect. And the man up here thought: ‘God should punish him.’ The little hammer was lying next to him, because the blacksmith had been doing some work in the church. And then, for one moment, he believed he was God. He picked up the hammer, and he let it fall.”

Wilfred Bohun began to shake. Then, suddenly, he cried. “Yes,” he said. “It was me. I don’t know what came over me. For one minute I felt like the hand of God. And then I was a murderer. I came down and I tried to blame poor Joe. I am a wicked man.”
“How did you know?” he asked after a while.
“I am only a man, and so I know what men can do,” said Father Brown. “And I knew that the blacksmith was innocent. He was too sure of God. A guilty man is never so calm.”

Wilfred looked over the wall. For a moment, Father Brown was afraid that he would jump. He put his hand on his arm. “Don’t,” he said. “That door leads to hell. Go down the stairs, not over the wall. Go down to the people.”
“What will you do?” asked Wilfred. “Will you go to the police?”
“No,” said Father Brown. “I will say nothing. I am a priest, not a policeman. You must decide what to do yourself. But I think you know what is right.”

The two men went down the long stairs together. At the bottom, Wilfred Bohun stopped and took a deep breath. Then, without a word, he walked slowly across the street towards the police station, to confess. Father Brown watched him go, and the evening sun shone on the old grey tower above them.
